_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-29 03:18:38Z)**_

The short answer: DeadReckon has built much of the hard execution kernel, but it has not yet delivered the complete original experience.

Today it is a serious local verified-run system. It is not yet a dependable “start this goal, walk away, and trust it to keep working until the goal is genuinely complete” product.

## Where the project stands

| Original promise | Current state | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Define “done” before starting | Plain English can be compiled into `acceptance.yaml`; an LLM critic looks for weak checks and goals a stub could satisfy | Strong, although users can still fall back to detected project tests instead of consciously approving a real contract |
| Run coding CLIs in isolation | Git worktree and copy isolation are mature; changes require deliberate promotion | Strong for source isolation |
| Keep running until the goal is met | A normal run is foreground and limited to 12 turns; recovery normally requires `resume`. Chain has detached execution; current uncommitted plan work adds orphan adoption | Major remaining gap |
| Independently judge completion | A separate gate runs deterministic checks and validates the completion marker | Strong deterministic floor, but not the semantic meta-judge described in the original vision |
| Resist a dishonest worker | The worker cannot bypass a failing test merely by claiming completion; tamper checks catch several forms of weakening | Useful protection, but current “cannot forge” language overstates the boundary |
| Capture the whole run | State, snapshots, events, traces, spend, provenance, implementation notes and reports are persisted | One of the strongest parts of the system |
| Make the experience pleasant | The default five-command interface is quite good | Internally, too many execution models and advanced commands still leak into the mental model |

The most important correction is about the judge. The LLM currently helps write and critique the definition of done in [acceptance.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/acceptance.rs:642). Final acceptance is then deterministic. There is no independent LLM reading the original goal, the resulting change and the evidence and deciding whether the goal was semantically achieved.

That means the original `/goal` idea is only partly present: semantic judgment happens before execution, not at the final boundary.

The current run loop also has a real ceiling: normal runs configure 12 turns in [run.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/run.rs:496), after which the loop fails with a budget-exhausted state. State is durable, but the worker is not automatically durable. If its supervising process disappears, the job waits for an operator to resume or adopt it.

## What has genuinely been achieved

DeadReckon now has a credible “verified run” primitive:

1. Create an isolated workspace.
2. establish a completion contract;
3. run a chosen coding CLI;
4. retain state and evidence after every turn;
5. respond to gate failures with another corrective turn;
6. accept only after the external gate passes;
7. deliberately promote or export the result.

That is substantial. The current working tree passed the complete workspace test suite: 2,049 tests passed and none failed. I did not modify the repository.

The evidence system is also unusually thorough. [RunView](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/run_view.rs:20) gives a useful read model over persisted state and ledgers. The promotion boundary in [promotion.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/promotion.rs:25) makes “completed” meaningfully different from “applied to my repository.”

So this is not a speculative pile of commands. It contains a real, tested kernel.

## Necessary complexity

These are inherent to the product and should remain:

- Safely isolating and later promoting source changes.
- Supporting different CLI providers and their different streaming, cancellation and accounting behaviour.
- Durable job identity, state, locking, recovery and cancellation.
- Compiling acceptance criteria into executable checks.
- A semantic judge for requirements that cannot be reduced to tests.
- Preventing the worker from modifying its own acceptance mechanism.
- Recording enough evidence to explain why a result was accepted.
- Scheduling dependent and parallel units of verified work.
- Explicit budgets, deadlines and blocked states. “Until done” must not mean “loop forever.”

## Incidental complexity

This is complexity created by the current shape of the implementation rather than the underlying problem:

- Forty-five top-level command variants, even though most are hidden from ordinary help.
- Several overlapping journey concepts: run, chain, plan/fork/merge, campaign, reshape and others.
- Control truth spread across state JSON, several JSONL ledgers and sidecar files, requiring hand-written reconciliation and orphan adoption.
- Repeated provider, retry, narration and budget policies in different orchestration layers.
- Multiple documentation and narration pipelines.
- Compatibility aliases, no-op flags and old spellings.
- Making implementation-note production part of the completion ritual, rather than deriving the after-state account from captured evidence.
- Continuing to deepen campaigns, learning, narration and other secondary systems before unattended goal execution is fully dependable.

The architectural smell is: there is one good verified-run atom, but too many ways to arrange and supervise it.

## The trust-boundary problem

The README’s “it can’t fake the finish” claim is stronger than the current implementation warrants.

The gate nonce is stored inside the run directory, and the marker uses Rust’s `DefaultHasher` in [gate.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/gate.rs:752), rather than a cryptographic MAC or signature. General CLI-provider and Bash-tool execution do not consistently deny access to gate material. In addition, automatic sandbox selection can fall back to no sandbox.

The system can truthfully say:

> A separate process runs the acceptance checks, and an existing completion marker cannot make failing checks pass.

It cannot yet universally say:

> A hostile coding agent is technically unable to forge acceptance.

Results should distinguish:

- `VERIFIED + CONFINED`
- `VERIFIED + UNCONFINED`
- `NEEDS REVIEW`
- `FAILED`

That would make the confidence claim precise rather than absolute.

## Where I would take it next

### 1. Finish the durable goal executor

Make `deadreckon start` create a durable local job, return its ID and detach by default. A small supervisor or user service should:

- lease pending jobs;
- recover abandoned leases;
- restart after terminal or machine failure;
- retain bounded retry, spend and time policies;
- distinguish blocked, cancelled, budget-exhausted and failed;
- supervise runs, chains and plans through the same scheduler.

Temporal is the useful exemplar here. Its core model is a durable execution reconstructed from an append-only event history, with explicit lifecycle operations such as start, describe, result, cancel, terminate and reset. DeadReckon should extract those durability and operator-semantics patterns without becoming a distributed workflow platform. [Temporal workflow execution](https://docs.temporal.io/workflow-execution), [Temporal CLI workflow commands](https://docs.temporal.io/cli/command-reference/workflow).

### 2. Restore the semantic meta-judge as a second key

Completion should require:

1. Deterministic checks pass.
2. An independent, read-only semantic judge assesses the goal, contract, diff and evidence.

The semantic judge must never override failed deterministic checks. It should return `achieved`, `revise` or `uncertain`, with evidence-backed reasons. If it is unavailable in strict mode, the result becomes `NEEDS REVIEW`, not accepted.

This is necessary complexity: natural-language goals cannot always be completely compiled into tests.

### 3. Close the gate boundary

- Keep signing material outside the agent-visible workspace.
- Use HMAC-SHA-256 or a proper signature.
- Deny gate and proof paths across every provider and tool route.
- Bind the receipt to the contract, policy, source revision and resulting revision.
- Fail closed for unattended trusted runs.
- Add adversarial tests in which an agent deliberately searches for and attempts to forge the marker.

### 4. Collapse the product around one job model

Keep the ordinary surface:

```text
start
attach
status
list
finish
```

Plans, chains and campaigns should become internal scheduling shapes or an explicitly advanced namespace. They should all create the same durable jobs and verified-run receipts.

Similarly, create one append-only control event history and derive current state and `RunView` from it. Rich spend, trace and documentation evidence can remain separate, but lifecycle truth should have one source.

### 5. Freeze secondary expansion and dogfood the promise

Temporarily freeze deeper campaign features, learning/improve surfaces and additional narration variants. Test the core promise on 20–30 real tasks across multiple repositories and providers.

Measure:

- unattended verified completion rate;
- automatic recovery rate;
- false acceptance and false rejection;
- number of operator interventions;
- time required to understand the final result;
- supervision and judging cost.

Kill the terminal, worker and machine during these trials. Remove network access. Attempt to tamper with the gate. Run DeadReckon on DeadReckon itself.

## Bottom line

DeadReckon contains a strong, unusually well-tested verified-run kernel inside an overgrown product.

The next phase should not be more orchestration features. It should make one promise completely true:

> Give DeadReckon a goal and an approved definition of done. It will work in isolation, survive interruptions, stop for explicit bounded reasons, independently verify both the checks and the meaning of the result, and leave behind a clear receipt explaining what happened.

Once that experience is reliable and pleasant, the plans, chains and campaigns become valuable multipliers instead of competing product models.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-29 03:18:38Z)**_

I’ll unpack “finish the durable goal executor” in concrete DeadReckon terms: what it means, what changes for the user, and what it does not require. I’m using the teaching skill because this is an architectural concept tied directly to this workspace.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-29 03:18:38Z)**_

“Finish the durable goal executor” means making DeadReckon responsible for the job after the user starts it.

Right now, DeadReckon has durable records, but not fully durable execution.

## Today

A normal run behaves roughly like this:

```text
Your terminal
    ↓
deadreckon run
    ↓
coding CLI
    ↓
gate
```

The `deadreckon run` process is the supervisor. While that process is alive, it keeps giving the coding CLI turns and checking the result.

DeadReckon saves enough state to recover, but:

- closing the supervisor stops the work;
- restarting the computer stops the work;
- someone must run `resume`;
- a normal attempt stops after 12 turns;
- detached execution exists for chains, but is not the common execution model.

That is resumable execution: “we can pick up where we stopped.”

It is not yet durable execution: “DeadReckon continues to own the job until it reaches a legitimate stopping point.”

## The proposed experience

The user should be able to do this:

```bash
deadreckon start "Add password reset"
```

DeadReckon would:

1. Create the isolated workspace.
2. Prepare and approve the definition of done.
3. Record a durable job.
4. Return a run ID immediately.
5. Let a background supervisor carry on.

```text
Started run dr-4821
Workspace: isolated
Status: running
Attach: deadreckon attach dr-4821
```

The terminal is no longer responsible for keeping the work alive.

```text
Terminal                 DeadReckon supervisor
   │                              │
   ├── start goal ───────────────→│
   │←── run ID ───────────────────┤
   │                              ├── run coding CLI
   │                              ├── save evidence
   │                              ├── run gate
   │                              ├── retry if appropriate
   │                              └── finish or stop explicitly
   │
   └── may close safely
```

`attach` would only observe or interact with the job. Disconnecting would not stop it.

## What keeps it durable

The background supervisor needs four basic mechanisms.

### A durable queue

`start` writes the goal into a local queue before execution begins:

```text
Job: dr-4821
Goal: Add password reset
Contract: acceptance.yaml
State: queued
Budget: $20
Deadline: 4 hours
Workspace: /path/to/worktree
```

If no supervisor is currently running, DeadReckon starts one.

### Leases and heartbeats

When a supervisor takes a job, it records:

```text
dr-4821 is leased by process 9312 until 14:35:00
```

It renews that lease periodically.

If the process crashes, the lease expires. Another supervisor can safely adopt the job. This prevents both abandonment and two supervisors working the same job simultaneously.

The uncommitted plan changes currently in the repository are moving towards this kind of orphan adoption, but it should become a shared facility for every execution shape.

### Checkpoints after every important event

DeadReckon already persists much of this. The durable executor would formalize events such as:

```text
Job started
Turn 1 started
Turn 1 completed
Gate failed
Corrective turn requested
Turn 2 completed
Gate passed
Semantic judge passed
Run verified
```

After a crash, the replacement supervisor reads this history and knows what to do next. It does not start the entire job again.

### Explicit stopping reasons

“Keep running until done” should not mean infinite retries.

A job may stop because it is:

```text
VERIFIED
BLOCKED — requires user decision
BUDGET_EXHAUSTED
DEADLINE_REACHED
FAILED — unrecoverable error
CANCELLED
```

Those states are part of the confidence model. Quietly dying because a terminal closed is not.

## It does not require a large distributed system

This could initially be a small local service:

```text
deadreckond
```

On macOS it could run through `launchd`; Linux could use a user-level `systemd` service. DeadReckon could also begin with a simpler detached conductor process, provided it has leases and automatic adoption.

It does not need Kubernetes, a server database or a cloud account. SQLite or an append-only local event log would be sufficient.

## Why this is the highest-priority gap

The original promise is not primarily “we save excellent records.” It is:

> Give the system a goal and trust it to carry responsibility for reaching a verified conclusion.

Without a durable executor, the human still carries part of that responsibility:

- keeping the process alive;
- noticing that it stopped;
- deciding whether to resume;
- restarting orchestration after a crash.

With it, the human only intervenes when DeadReckon produces an intentional `BLOCKED` state.

A practical definition of done for this feature would include:

- Start a run and close the terminal: it continues.
- Kill the coding CLI: DeadReckon retries or records a clear failure.
- Kill the supervisor: another supervisor adopts the run.
- Restart the computer: unfinished jobs resume automatically.
- Never run the same turn twice concurrently.
- Respect spend, time and retry limits.
- Preserve the same run ID, workspace and evidence throughout.
- Finish only through the normal verification boundary.

That change would turn DeadReckon from a well-persisted foreground runner into the “start it and trust it” product described in the original goal.

Read-only diagnosis complete. No files were edited.

The recent Graph commits materially improve the starting point: DeadReckon already has most of the execution engine needed for one durable job model. The right move is to wrap and consolidate the existing graph executor, not build another scheduler beside it.

`origin/main` and local `HEAD` both point to `da49212`.

## What the latest commits changed

The Graph series added:

- retries that preserve remaining spend and wall budgets;
- retry continuation from the failed run’s tree;
- gate-authored corrective reasons;
- plan-conductor crash recovery and orphan adoption;
- sequential per-node application;
- nested subplans;
- graph-shaped start classification;
- chains in the common inventory;
- one shared undo entry point.

The existing `Plan` executor is therefore the closest working sibling for the future scheduler. It already expresses:

- parallel and dependent nodes;
- sequential execution through `ApplyWhen::PerNode`;
- retries and circuit breakers;
- failure policies;
- nested subplans;
- isolated child runs;
- merge and promotion.

The intentional difference should be:

> Same graph executor, but owned by a durable `Job` supervisor instead of a foreground command.

## Current end-to-end trace

### Start

[`LaunchPlan`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/course.rs:218) is already a durable, approved launch decision containing the goal, shape, graph pieces, providers, budget and done-contract summary.

[`start_command`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/start.rs:2611) constructs it, but [`dispatch_start_command`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/start.rs:2860) still calls one of several synchronous command families:

- run;
- extend;
- campaign;
- orchestrate review/full-plan.

Afterward, `start` scans the filesystem to discover which new run or plan appeared. It does not create one durable outer identity before dispatch.

### Identity and ordinary commands

Shakedown’s [`ResolvedRef`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/reference.rs:85) and [`resolve_ref`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/reference.rs:304) are a strong consolidation precedent.

They let the ordinary commands recognize runs, plan children, plans, chains and campaigns, but the commands still branch by underlying kind:

- [`attach_command`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/attach.rs:28)
- [`status_command`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/main.rs:10973)
- [`show_command`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/main.rs:10536)
- [`list_command`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/inspection.rs:4)
- [`finish_command`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/lifecycle.rs:57)

`list` now combines runs, plans and chains. It still does not include campaigns because campaigns have neither the common record nor a scope. `finish` has different result-resolution rules for each shape.

### Lifecycle truth

There are currently four state machines:

- [`PipelineState` and `RunStatus`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/state.rs:23)
- `Plan` and `PlanStatus`
- `Chain` and `ChainStatus`
- `Campaign` and `CampaignStatus`

There are also four event streams:

- run `events.jsonl`;
- `plan-events.jsonl`;
- `chain-events.jsonl`;
- `campaign-events.jsonl`.

Run [`RunEventKind`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-protocol/src/ledger.rs:13) is mainly activity telemetry. It does not contain enough transitions to reconstruct `PipelineState`. State changes are written separately through `save_state`.

Plans are closer to the desired design. [`PlanEventKind`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/plan.rs:556) covers meaningful lifecycle edges, and [`append_plan_event`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/plan.rs:857) creates an append-only history. The plan feed replays that file, discovers child run streams and folds them into one view.

### Read models and receipts

[`RunView`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/run_view.rs:25) is the strongest existing read-model sibling. It joins state, events, spend, traces, snapshots, docs, sandbox facts and gate proof into one projection. [`report_command`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/report.rs:12) renders it deterministically.

It is leaf-run-only.

Helm has already prototyped the broader projection:

- [`SPINE_CONTRACT_TABLE`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/tui/spine.rs:83) asks the same five questions of every shape.
- `spine_for_run`, `spine_for_plan`, `spine_for_chain` and `spine_for_campaign` implement those questions separately.
- [`AttachTarget`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/tui/tree.rs:20) and [`build_tree`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/tui/tree.rs:244) already build one operator tree across all shapes.

This is the exact seam for `JobView`: move the common meaning out of the TUI and make it the core read model.

### Existing supervision patterns

Reuse these rather than redesigning them:

- Detached chain conductor: [`detach_chain_conductor`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/chain/mod.rs:1486)
- Chain conductor and heartbeats: [`run_chain_conductor`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/chain/mod.rs:753)
- Shared filesystem lock and heartbeat: [`acquire_lock`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/lock.rs:91)
- Plan re-entry and conductor liveness: [`fork_command`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/plan.rs:1814)
- Orphan reconciliation: [`adopt_orphaned_children`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/plan.rs:2514)

These prove crash recovery is possible, but it is currently initiated manually by rerunning `fork` or `resume`.

## Recommended object model

The user-facing hierarchy should become:

```text
Job
└── execution graph
    └── one or more run attempts
```

A `Job` is what the operator starts, lists, attaches to, finishes and receives a receipt for.

A `Plan` becomes the internal execution graph.

A `Run` remains one isolated coding-agent attempt and retains all of its rich evidence.

### Durable job files

```text
~/.deadreckon/jobs/<job-id>/
├── job.json
├── launch-plan.json
├── job-events.jsonl
├── lease.json
└── receipt.json
```

`job.json` should contain only stable identity and policy:

- job ID;
- scope;
- goal;
- graph/root reference;
- launch-plan reference and digest;
- done-contract reference and digest;
- budget/deadline/retry policy;
- creation time.

The job ID should also be the visible root run/plan ID where practical. Do not introduce one user-visible job ID plus a second root execution ID.

### One append-only control history

Add `JobEvent` to `deadreckon-protocol`, following Keel’s ownership rule for persisted ledger types.

Useful events include:

```text
created
queued
lease_acquired
attempt_started
attempt_stopped
retry_scheduled
deterministic_gate_passed
deterministic_gate_failed
semantic_judge_achieved
semantic_judge_revise
semantic_judge_uncertain
blocked
budget_exhausted
deadline_reached
cancel_requested
cancelled
failed
verified
result_applied
result_exported
```

Each event should carry:

- schema version;
- job ID;
- monotonically increasing sequence;
- timestamp;
- idempotency/causation key;
- bounded details and evidence references.

Do not put tool calls, spend rows or provider chatter into this stream. Those existing ledgers remain attached to leaf runs. “One lifecycle history” should mean one place answers what happened to the job, not one enormous log containing every byte.

`lease.json` may hold frequently renewed operational lease data. Only meaningful ownership transitions need to enter the durable lifecycle history.

### `JobView`

Add a core `JobView` that reduces `job-events.jsonl` and links to:

- the approved `LaunchPlan`;
- current lease/liveness;
- graph/tree progress;
- child `RunView` projections;
- deterministic gate evidence;
- semantic assessment;
- canonical result run;
- delivery/apply/export records;
- missing or corrupt evidence.

`RunView` should remain intact as the leaf evidence model. `JobView` composes it.

Then route `status`, `list`, `show`, `attach`, `finish` and `report` through `JobView`.

## Phased migration

### P0 — Characterize current journeys

Before schema work, pin:

- every start shape’s returned ID;
- list/status/show/attach/finish agreement;
- current JSON schemas and plain output;
- plan, chain and campaign terminal/result semantics;
- legacy directory discovery.

The Shakedown cross-verb journey test is the working sibling.

### P1 — Job protocol and legacy projection

Add:

- `deadreckon-protocol/src/job.rs`;
- `deadreckon-core/src/job.rs`;
- job path helpers;
- event reducer;
- checked `job-view.schema.json`.

Legacy runs/plans/chains/campaigns should load through adapters without modifying their directories. Mark their control history as `legacy_snapshot`; do not invent events that never occurred.

Depth tests:

- `job_event_sequence_reduces_deterministically`
- `duplicate_event_id_is_idempotent`
- `event_gap_is_reported_not_hidden`
- `legacy_run_projects_without_writes`
- `legacy_plan_chain_campaign_keep_their_ids`
- `job_view_schema_is_checked`

### P2 — One read model

Implement `JobView` and make list/status/show/report consume it.

Keep existing renderers initially; only replace their data source.

Depth tests:

- `list_contains_every_job_kind_including_campaign`
- `latest_is_the_first_listed_job`
- `job_view_run_facts_match_run_view`
- `job_view_primary_action_matches_existing_spine_for_each_kind`
- `report_for_plan_cites_child_run_proofs`
- `missing_optional_evidence_is_visible_not_fatal`

At the end, the four-way `SPINE_CONTRACT_TABLE` should no longer be necessary.

### P3 — Start creates and queues one job

Generate the job ID and persist `job.json`, launch plan and `created`/`queued` events before launching anything.

Replace before/after filesystem scans in `start`.

`start` should return immediately with the job ID. A supervisor claims it.

Depth tests:

- `start_persists_job_before_spawning_worker`
- `start_returns_one_id_for_single_plan_and_nested_graph`
- `closing_start_stdout_does_not_cancel_job`
- `direct_run_and_orchestrate_register_compatibility_jobs`
- `failed_spawn_leaves_a_visible_failed_job`

### P4 — Supervisor, leases and automatic adoption

Move the chain lock/heartbeat and plan orphan-adoption patterns into a shared job runner.

Depth tests:

- `dead_supervisor_lease_is_reclaimed`
- `live_supervisor_is_never_usurped`
- `reclaimed_job_does_not_run_one_attempt_twice`
- `completed_child_is_adopted_after_conductor_crash`
- `interrupted_child_retries_with_remaining_budget`
- `restart_requeues_only_nonterminal_jobs`
- `attach_disconnect_does_not_affect_execution`

### P5 — Collapse execution shapes

Use `Plan` as the common graph engine.

- Single run: one-node plan or direct one-leaf optimization.
- Ordered work: `ApplyWhen::PerNode`.
- Parallel work: `ApplyWhen::AtEnd`.
- Chain compatibility: translate chain steps into per-node graph policy while preserving hooks, undo and apply semantics.
- Campaign compatibility: translate into nested subplans only after preserving campaign roll-up and no-laundering guarantees.

Do not delete `chain.json` support immediately. Thirteen chain subcommands still read it. Route those through a compatibility adapter for one release before making old chain storage read-only.

### P6 — Receipt and dogfood metrics

Generate the final receipt from `JobView`, not generated narrative prose. Optional narration can polish it, but facts and citations come from the event/evidence model.

Existing [`LearningEpisodeMetrics`](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/learning.rs:46) already captures turns, wall time, spend, gate failures, doc warnings and rewinds. Extend the projection with:

- automatic recoveries;
- operator interventions;
- retry count;
- semantic revise/uncertain count;
- supervisor and judge overhead;
- final stop reason;
- confinement level.

Reuse the operator-only posture of `release/preflight-real.sh`, but make the new dogfood harness consume public `start --json`, job IDs and receipts instead of finding `state.json` and sleeping for fixed intervals.

## Compatibility risks

- Campaigns currently lack scope. Legacy campaign scope must be `unknown` or all-scopes; do not guess from the current directory.
- Current status enums do not distinguish blocked, budget-exhausted, deadline-reached and needs-review consistently. Preserve legacy wording instead of inferring precise states from arbitrary failure strings.
- Event/state dual writing can create another truth split. Transition APIs should append the event first and treat old state files as replayable scheduler checkpoints.
- Existing direct advanced verbs can bypass `start`. They must register jobs or remain explicitly legacy-only.
- Chain hooks, auto-apply, redo and undo are semantics, not presentation debt. A plan adapter must preserve them.
- Campaign roll-up and refusal propagation are trust invariants. Nested subplans alone do not replace them.
- `finish` currently means different things for leaf, plan, chain and campaign results. `JobView` needs an explicit canonical result and delivery record.
- `RunView` JSON is a checked public projection. Add `JobView`; do not silently mutate `RunView` into a different schema.
- Current JSONL append is synced but has no sequence number. Job control events need one writer per lease, sequence validation and idempotency keys.
- Existing homes must remain readable without bulk migration.

## Operator acceptance scenarios

The human acceptance script should eventually include:

1. Start a single goal; receive one ID within seconds.
2. Close the terminal; `status` shows the same job still running.
3. Kill the coding CLI; the supervisor records and retries it within policy.
4. Kill the supervisor; another supervisor adopts the same job without duplicate work.
5. Restart the machine; the unfinished job resumes automatically.
6. Exhaust spend, wall and retry limits separately; each produces the correct explicit stop reason.
7. Run a parallel graph, ordered graph and nested graph; all appear as jobs with the same five-command lifecycle.
8. Use legacy run, plan, chain and campaign IDs; they remain inspectable and finish/refuse honestly.
9. Disconnect and reconnect `attach`; execution is unaffected.
10. Finish a verified job; the receipt cites contract, checks, semantic assessment, child attempts, spend, source/result revisions and delivery.
11. Corrupt or remove optional narrative evidence; the factual receipt still renders with a missing-evidence warning.
12. Rebuild `JobView` from the append-only history and confirm it matches the saved projection byte-for-byte.

The central recommendation is therefore:

> Make `Job` the one operator object, `Plan` the one graph executor, and `RunView` the preserved leaf-evidence atom. Add one append-only job lifecycle above the existing rich ledgers instead of replacing or merging them.
